title: FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey Resigns Amid Bureau Shake-Up
snippet: Andrew Bailey, the former Missouri Attorney General brought in as FBI co-deputy director, has announced his resignation after a turbulent year at the bureau.
content:
WASHINGTON — FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey announced his resignation on Monday, marking the latest high-level departure in a turbulent period of leadership changes at the federal law enforcement agency.

Bailey, a staunch conservative loyalist and former Missouri attorney general, informed bureau employees via email that he is stepping down to spend more time with his family in Missouri. He later confirmed the news on social media, expressing pride in his tenure and backing FBI Director Kash Patel's vision for reforming the bureau.

A Non-Traditional Appointment

Brought into top leadership roughly a year ago, Bailey served as co-deputy director alongside former Secret Service agent and conservative podcaster Dan Bongino. The appointments were unprecedented, as neither man possessed prior FBI experience—a sharp departure for a role typically reserved for career bureau veterans tasked with managing daily operations.

Bongino stepped down earlier this year following reported frustrations over the demands of the position, and was replaced by career FBI official Christopher Raia.

Controversy and Internal Shifts

Bailey's time at the FBI coincided with substantial internal friction, including a wave of dismissals and reassignments of experienced career agents. Most recently, two top counterterrorism agents in the Washington field office were transferred after leadership reportedly grew dissatisfied with the pace of an investigation into threats against conservative podcaster Katie Miller, wife of senior White House aide Stephen Miller.

Bailey also raised eyebrows within the law enforcement community in January when he personally appeared on-site as FBI agents executed search warrants to seize 2020 election materials in Fulton County, Georgia. It is exceptionally rare for an agency deputy director to personally oversee routine investigative steps, particularly in a case tangled with political sensitivities.

Before joining the bureau, Bailey made a name for himself as Missouri's attorney general by championing conservative legal battles against corporate diversity programs, sanctuary city policies, and youth transgender care.
